title: How We Learn From Errors
author: Jonathan Firth
summary: Jonathan Firth traces the shift in educational thinking away from 'errorless learning,' the traditional behaviourist-influenced assumption that teachers should structure practice in tiny steps so students never make mistakes, for fear a wrong response would become an ingrained habit. He credits Ausubel, Rosenshine and Hunter with popularising the small-steps, error-avoidant approach, and notes it isn't baseless: badly ingrained habits genuinely can be hard to correct. But he presents Janet Metcalfe's 2017 review paper as the more complete picture, arguing that avoiding errors entirely makes practice artificially easy and predictable, forfeiting real benefits: an error can be informative, helping a learner course-correct, and sometimes understanding only clicks after getting something wrong. Firth explains that mistakes can become explicit, episodic memories, recallable life-event-like memories, that aid the kind of reflective, explanatory questioning ('why was I wrong?') that's independently evidence-based as a learning technique. He closes by inviting readers to consider whether desirable difficulties inevitably produce errors as a byproduct, and whether the answer might vary by subject or age group, rather than presenting Metcalfe's conclusion as a settled, universal rule.
points: Firth traces errorless learning to Ausubel, Rosenshine and Hunter's behaviourist-influenced concern that uncorrected wrong responses become ingrained habits, giving the older position real intellectual grounding rather than a strawman.

He presents Janet Metcalfe's 2017 review as the counterargument: avoiding errors makes practice artificially easy and predictable, forfeiting the informative, course-correcting value an error can provide.

He connects error-based learning to explicit, episodic memory, arguing a mistake can become a recallable 'memory of a life event' that supports the independently evidence-based technique of explanatory questioning ('why was I wrong?').
He closes without fully resolving the tension, explicitly asking readers whether desirable difficulties inevitably produce errors as a byproduct and whether the answer varies by subject or age group.
quotes: It may seem obvious that fewer mistakes equates to better learning, but sometimes, the opposite is true.
A traditional assumption across education is that it would be best if learners avoid making any errors at all, that their practice is errorless.
In a review paper, Janet Metcalfe argued that avoiding errors is unnecessary and can even be counterproductive, as it tends to lead to practice being easy and predictable.
An error can be informative, helping a learner to course-correct. Sometimes, you don’t understand something until you get it wrong.
A mistake can stick in one's memory as an explicit, episodic memory. These are memories of life events, things that we can recall and reflect on.
Overall, the big idea in the paper is that schools and education systems have shied away from errors and mistakes, and that this should change.
